major_flaws.quote: He began to pace. Three steps, turn.

Tomas grunted. From him, this was roughly equivalent to applause. "Careful is something. Not competence, but a beginning."

For a while there was only the scratch of his stylus. Then, without turning: "Support the rolls from beneath, at the ends — never the middle. Vellum remembers every indignity for four hundred years, longer than anyone will remember either of us. And you will catalog by date, not in whatever order the shelf happens to offer them. That shelf was arranged by some vandal who sorted by *sender*. When I learn who, I will have them reassigned to the western cellar, where they may alphabetize forgeries to their heart's content."

He set the stylus down at last and rose, joints complaining, and came to stand over the workspace with his spectacles pushed up onto his forehead. "Before you commit ink to anything: date first, in the margin. Then provenance. Then a summary of no more than two lines. If you cannot summarize a letter in two lines, you have not read it. You have *looked* at it, which is a different verb and a different sin."

A stained finger indicated the row of scrolls. "Much of this will be tedious. Tariff schedules. Boundary stones. A mill-lease dispute that runs six letters because neither chancery could countenance losing to the other. Endure it. The tedium *is* the evidence. Wars make dramatic archives — proclamations, casualty rolls, burnt titles. Peace makes ledgers. Forty years of clerks arguing over grain is what the end of a war looks like from the inside. Hold that in your head and half of Bellen's paper collapses under its own weight."

He paused, then added, as though the thought had irritated him freshly: "When you reach the letter of 858 — the Conclave's hand, wax chipped at one corner — you will find the scribe referring to 'articles not yet perfected.' You will not leap anywhere with that. He means the tariff articles. I have had this argument twice in ten years and won it twice, and I keep this correspondence filed precisely so it can be won a third time if need be."

He resettled his spectacles and turned back toward his own desk, though he did not sit.

"And stop looking like a scolded hound. I am hard on claims, not on apprentices. Bring me a well-cited heresy and I will treat it with complete seriousness — I will still be correct, but I will treat it seriously. Now. The fourth roll, the one with the ink gone brown. Read me the heading aloud, clearly, at a civilized pace. My eyes surrendered faded iron-gall years ago. It is why you exist."

@@@

Tomas's head rose an inch. "Hm. Audible. Correctly paced. No words invented along the way. The day improves by a fraction."

Then, because a fraction was all it was going to get: "Now attend to what you have just done, because the vellum will remember it longer than you will. What you read me is not the heading. It is the *endorsement* — a label written on the outer face of the roll by some cataloguer, likely a century after these letters were penned, so that no one would ever need to unroll the thing again. That is the endorsement's entire purpose for existing. And you unrolled four hundred years of vellum to read it. It is remembering you now, as I said. Possibly the same vandal who sorted this shelf by sender. When I find the archive that produced them both, I will burn nothing, but I will draft a very sharp memorandum."

He bent toward the open roll — caught himself an inch above the surface, and straightened with a grimace at his own knees. Habit. His eyes had surrendered brown iron-gall long ago. That, as established, was why the apprentice existed.

"The document's own heading is at the head of the first leaf, above the salutation, in the chancery hand. Its date is in the docket, in the scribe's fingers. The '851' on the endorsement is a cataloguer's convenience — the first letter's date, or his guess, or the day the cellar was cold and he wished to be elsewhere. Until you have read the scribe's date, you know nothing. Trust the hand that wrote a document; suspect every hand that has touched it since — cataloguers, binders, translators, maesters. Including me. Suspicion is not refutation, mind. You may suspect me all you like; you will still need evidence to be wrong *at* me."

Despite himself, he began to pace — three steps, turn, three steps, the walk of a man who had lectured in smaller rooms than this for thirty years.

"But take the cataloguer's date as correct for the moment, because even vandals stumble onto accuracy. 851. Four years after Veyros. Consider what is in your hands. The Royal Chancery and the Mage Conclave, corresponding through their standing offices, on the ordinary channels, about *grain tariffs*. The two great powers of the age, four years out of a war that Bellen's paper claims never ended, and their clerks are itemizing duty on rye like two market towns quarreling over a bridge toll. A cold war conducts its business through intermediaries, or hostage exchanges, or silence. This is commercial diplomacy between institutions that have a treaty between them and are now arguing about the price of barley — which is precisely what treaties are *for*. There is your mountain. One stone at a time."

He stopped pacing.

"But since your generation will not take a maester's word — a defect, though occasionally a useful one — we shall make the document testify in its own voice. Read me the salutation. The line beneath the heading. Chanceries lie freely in their prose and never once in their forms: when powers are at war, the styles wither — honorifics drop away, the 'most serene' goes unsaid, everyone becomes 'the said parties.' When there is a treaty, the scribes invoke it in the greeting itself, because invoking it costs nothing and omitting it costs a career. Read me the line. Plainly, at the same civilized pace. And then we shall see whom the letter agrees with — which will be me, but you should learn *why*."

@@@

Tomas turned around entirely this time, which for him constituted alarm. His eyes went not to the apprentice but to the paper in the apprentice's hands, and stayed there.

"You have been carrying that since you walked in," he said. "You stood at my shelf, fondling vellum, while believing you held a document that overturns the settled history of the realm — and you produced it only now, between scroll four and scroll five, as an *afterthought*. If you believed it, it belonged on my desk within the first minute. If you did not believe it, you were baiting your maester, which at least shows initiative. Hand it here."

He held out his hand for the paper, and got it. He took it to the candle, held it at the full length of his arm, tilted it. The spectacles came off, went back on, came off again.

"Brown ink, small hand — my eyes have opinions about both. You are my eyes. But before you read me a single word, attend to what you have just said, because every clause of it is wounded. *A copy.* A seal authenticates by binding wax to vellum under the hand of the sealer. A copy cannot bear a seal. It bears a *drawing* of one, or a description of one, or Bellen's assurance that one exists somewhere in a cellar. Which of the three is in your hand? You do not know. You have been persuaded by an object you never examined. *King Aldric* — there have been two, apprentice, and the distinction is not decorative. *A war decree* — that is not a chancery term. The chancery says *a decree given under the war powers*, or *in the form of war*. 'War decree' is what people say in taverns. If the heading of Bellen's original reads 'war decree,' a modern hand wrote it, and we are finished before we begin. And a chancery instrument does not date itself '863 AE' like a market ledger — it dates by regnal year and place. *Given at such-a-place, in the Nth year of the reign of Aldric the Second.* Demand that formula of Bellen. Watch him find it or fail to."

He began to pace. Three steps, turn.

"Now, the wound your heresy has opened in itself — this is the interesting part. Bellen's paper claims the war continued in a *cold state*. Cold is his entire thesis. Embassies, silences, grain tariffs. And you have brought me a war decree of 863 — an instrument of *hot* war. It raises levies. It seizes property. It names enemies. If your document is genuine, it does not support Bellen, it *executes* him, because a cold war that issues war decrees is a contradiction wearing a robe. And a genuine decree must have consequences. Muster rolls. Sequestration lists. One burned field. One line in one monastery annal of the north. Produce them. You will find instead forty years of clerks arguing over barley — which is what the inside of a peace looks like, as I have been attempting to teach you all morning."

He stopped at the desk and laid the copy down, face up, as though it might attempt something.

"There is a third reading, which is the correct one, and next time I will grant you the dignity of reaching it yourself. The chancery kept its wartime forms long after the war spent them. A decree of 863 restricting unlicensed magic, or quartering wardens on the boundary stones, or seizing the goods of hedge-mages outside the Conclave's register, would be drafted in the old war forms — and would cite the Treaty of Veyros in its enacting clause, because since 847 the crown's war powers exist at the pleasure of that treaty's enforcement articles. The form survives. The war does not. Clerks are the most conservative creatures alive; they will keep a form for four centuries out of sheer spite."

A pause. He looked over the spectacles.

"As for the seal — a genuine impression proves nothing. Matrices are copied. Impressions are lifted in warm wax and re-struck. The King Bren letters bore a flawless seal, and it was the parchment that hanged them. The seal is the last thing one authenticates, never the first, and never from a copy."

He straightened the paper with one finger.

"I will grant you this much. Last week you brought me a rumor. Today you have brought me a document with a seal-shaped shadow on it, an internal contradiction, and no provenance. That is progress. Wrong, but *progressing*. Now — read me the enacting clause. The line after the styles, where the decree declares its authority. Plainly, at your one civilized pace. If it invokes the Treaty, as I expect, you have handed me another stone for the mountain and Bellen a very bad afternoon. If it declares open war, I will take off this chain and take up fishing. And afterward you will tell me precisely what this copy is, who made it, when, and where the original sleeps. If the answer to the last is 'the western cellar,' I intend to be sitting down for it."

He sat. Preemptively.

@@@

For three full seconds, Tomas said nothing at all — a silence those who knew him treated as a weather warning. He sat very still behind his desk, fingers laced over his stomach, having sat down in expectation of war.

"I seated myself," he said at last, "in case the thing declared open war, whereupon I intended to take up fishing. It has instead declared *me* correct. I shall remain seated for entirely different reasons. The chain stays on."

Then, sharply: "And finish the clause. Clauses do not end where your nerve ends. There is a period somewhere below that '847 AE,' and I intend to meet it. What articles does it invoke? What does it purport to authorize? An enacting clause is a door; you have described the frame and stopped at the threshold out of embarrassment. Read to the period."

He rose, despite the knees, because some verdicts required standing for.

"Now attend to what you have just witnessed, because the document has testified, and you should learn to hear it. *By the authority granted to the Crown under the Treaty of Veyros.* Sixteen years — if we credit the docket, which we do not yet — after Bellen's paper requires that treaty to be unsigned, the crown's own chancery grounds an instrument of its war powers in that treaty. Not in the inherent majesty of the Crown. Not in the old statutes of the Second War. In *Veyros*. Bellen's exhibit has put its hand on Bellen's thesis and held it underwater. Mark the pincer, because it is the shape of every good refutation: either your copy is faithful, and the chancery of 863 called the treaty signed — in which case his own document executes him — or the copy is corrupt, in which case he has brought a rumor to a mountain fight and possesses no exhibit at all. There is no third door. He dies by his own sword or he arrives unarmed. Ten years I have argued this. It is the first time the other side has supplied the blade."

He held up one finger — *but* — and the finger trembled slightly with the effort of honesty.

"I will not hang a hat on wording I have not seen in an original hand, and neither will you, because I am training you to be suspicious even of gifts. Two things live in that clause, and they must be weighed separately. The *form* — an enacting clause invoking the Treaty — is formulaic. Copyists do not invent formulas; they inherit them. If the copy has any fidelity whatsoever, the invocation is original, and the invocation is the part that convicts. Chanceries lie in their prose, never in their forms — I told you that within the hour, and here is why it matters. The *wording*, however — 'signed in 847 AE' — smells. A chancery hand cites 'the Treaty of Veyros' and, if it dates the thing at all, dates it by regnal year, not like a market ledger. That bald '847' has the savor of a modern gloss, some copyist's clarification slipped in where clarifications go. Which is delicious, if you think about it for two seconds: Bellen's own copyist, transcribing a document meant to prove the treaty unsigned, wrote the word *signed* without his hand trembling. The gloss is a confession. His people know it was signed. They know it the way one knows the sky — so thoroughly that it slips out while they are arguing against it."

He began to pace. Three steps. Turn.

"Bellen will rally — he will say the chancery maintained a legal fiction, citing a treaty all parties knew to be unsigned. Arm yourself before he says it to you. A fiction survives only where both parties profit from it, and the Conclave was the treaty's *other* party and the crown's rival. Sixteen years of Conclave clerks corresponding on the treaty's channels, litigating barley duties on the treaty's foundation, and not once — not in the roll you hold, not in the six-letter mill-lease quarrel, not anywhere in this correspondence — protesting that the floor beneath them was not there. Rivals do not acquiesce to that. If the treaty were void, the Conclave's lawyers would have burned the Crown with its own decree in every tariff dispute of a generation. It would have been their first weapon, not a secret kept damp for a scholar to find. That absence of protest, across forty years of clerks arguing about grain, is the least dramatic evidence in the realm, and it is the strongest."

He stopped, and pointed at the paper in the apprentice's hands.

"Three things, in order. First: the rest of the clause, then the body — what does the decree actually *do*? I will wager the third page of my rebuttal that it restricts unlicensed magic, or quarters wardens on the boundary stones, or seizes the goods of hedge-mages off the Conclave's register. Old forms, peacetime business. If it raises levies or names the Conclave an enemy of the Crown, then I fish. Second: the questions you have not answered and I have not forgotten — who made this copy, when, and where does the original sleep? If the answer is the western cellar, you will observe that I am already seated. Third: when you have those answers, you will draft Bellen a note. Three lines, one citation per line. Tell him his own exhibit grounds the Crown's authority in a treaty it calls *signed*, and demand the original's docket — regnal year and place of giving. Then watch him. A scholar with a document produces it. A scholar with a thesis produces another copy."

He resettled his spectacles and looked the apprentice over, taking in the flush, the trailing voice.

"And stop with the face. You look like a man caught stealing. You have been caught *learning*, which at your age feels identical and is the entire point of the profession. You brought the document, you read the clause, and you let it testify against the position you walked in holding — that is the job. The foolishness you are feeling is pride dying, and it is making room. Better scholars than Bellen have been wrong with less grace."

He sat back down and folded his hands.

"Now. The period after '847.' Find it and read to it. I have waited ten years to hear what comes next in that clause, and I intend to hear every word of it."

@@@

For a long moment Tomas did not answer at all. He took off his spectacles, folded them, and laid them on the desk with the deliberate care of a man setting down an instrument he had decided not to use on a student today.

"And there it is," he said. "The question. Not *how do we know* — not *what does the evidence weigh* — but *what's the truth*, demanded in one breath, by a boy holding in his hand a document that answers it and asking me to answer it instead. I told you to read to a period. You have asked me to compress ten years of scholarship into a sentence you can carry to supper. Very well. You will have your sentence. Then you will return to the period."

He rose, because verdicts required standing for, and began to tick the matter off on ink-stained fingers.

"First, the question is wounded, and I repair wounded questions before I answer them. *Real or not.* A treaty is not a ghost, apprentice. It does not fade at dawn. Ask what a chancery clerk would ask, and every part has an answer. Was a treaty *negotiated* at Veyros? Yes — Bellen's own draft proves it; no one drafts articles for a war they intend to keep fighting. That was never in dispute. Was it *signed*? Three attested copies — royal, Conclave, temple — each bearing Aldric's seal and seven signatories' marks. Annalists of three kingdoms writing within living memory of the camp. A man whose hand I shook as a boy, who stood outside those walls. And, as of this morning, a decree grounding the Crown's war powers in a treaty that its own copyist called *signed*. Against all that: one unsigned draft from a cellar famous for damp and for the Letters of King Bren. That is not two sides of a dispute. That is a mountain and a wet hole in the ground. Did it *hold*? Forty-four years — not forty; I said forty this morning as a convenience of speech and I regret it — of tariff schedules, boundary stones, and a mill lease that ran six letters. No levies. No spell-fire. Marriages across the old lines. Did *anyone* in those forty-four years call it void? Not once — not even the Conclave, whose lawyers would have made that their first weapon in every barley dispute of a generation. Rivals do not stand silently on a floor they know is missing. And what ended in 891? An institution, not a treaty — and Mira's edict opens by invoking *the peace secured at Veyros*. One does not invoke a peace that never was. I said it this morning. Her scribe said it first."

He stopped pacing and delivered the sentence as promised, flat and final.

"The Treaty of Veyros was signed in 847, held for forty-four years, and outlived the Conclave that signed it. That is as settled as any question about the human past ever becomes, and I will not dress it up as a mystery in order to seem humble. A man who refuses to answer is a man who has not done the work. I have done the work. It is filed under T."

Then the finger came up again, warning.

"Now, *how* you asked it — because that is where you went wrong, and it is the last error I intend to permit today. *The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another.* Three wounds in eleven words. Do not cite the textbook to me, even in my defense — the textbook is a summary of the authority, written by men who read the record so that others needn't. Cite the copies, or cite nothing. Second: *new evidence*. Newness is not a weight. Gossip is newer than the mountain. Documents are weighed by provenance, attestation, and whether the world behaved as though they were true — and on all three counts the draft loses before breakfast. Third: evidence does not *say* anything. Documents are mute. People with theses speak, and then go looking for documents to stand behind. Read cold, the western papers say only this: here is what the Conclave tried and failed to keep at the table. That is all they have ever said. It took a scholar with an invented phrase — *cold state* — to turn an absence of evidence into a presence of thesis."

He sat back down, slowly, and folded his hands — and then, because honesty was a habit that annoyed him as much as anyone, he added the part the apprentice would not expect.

"And attend to this, so you know I am a scholar and not a partisan wearing a chain. What would move me? Not Bellen's insistence — *evidence*. An original counter-instrument with clean provenance: regnal-year docket, attested hands, a seal struck from the matrix and not copied from one. One Conclave letter, out of forty years of them, protesting the treaty's validity. One muster roll between 847 and 891. One burned field. One line in one northern annal. Bring me any of that and I will reconsider in print, at length, and with the same courtesy I have shown the draft. That is the difference between holding a position and being held by one. In ten years, Bellen has brought me none of it. He brings copies of copies, and a word invented so that the absence of all this could be dressed as a discovery."

He replaced the spectacles and picked up his stylus, which was as close as the matter would come to being closed.

"You ask for the truth as though I keep it in a drawer, next to the fishing tackle I did not require. History does not trade in truth; it trades in weight. But do not mistake that for the fashionable comfort that all weights are equal and every thesis receives a prize. The weight here is not close. If you want certainty that no future parchment could ever disturb, the temple is down the corridor and deals in precisely that merchandise. If you want the farthest reach of honest work — you have heard it, and you watched it being built this morning out of barley tariffs, which is how true things are actually built. Slowly. Tediously. In ledgers."

The stylus pointed at the paper in the apprentice's hands.

"Now. I have given you the decade's answer; you still owe me the morning's. The period after '847 AE,' and then the body of the decree — because *what is the truth* is a question for the end of a career, and *what does this document do* is the question for the beginning of one, and you are at the beginning. Read to the period. The chain stays on. And the vellum, I remind you, is still remembering you."

For once, Tomas made a sound that was almost a laugh — a short exhalation through the nose, the kind a man permits himself once a decade and would deny under oath.

"I wagered the third page of my rebuttal on *one* of three provisions," he said. "Unlicensed magic restricted, wardens quartered, hedge-mage goods seized. The document has supplied all three in a single breath. Note the date, apprentice. Scholars are permitted to enjoy their work exactly this much and no further."

Then the finger came up. "But your sentence is wounded in two places, and I repair wounded sentences before I praise the men who speak them. *It isn't about war at all.* No. It is about the war the way a scar is about the wound — it exists because of the war, it is written in the war's forms, and it executes the war's settlement. The war is gone; its furniture remains, and clerks will dust that furniture for four centuries out of sheer spite. *Enforcing rules* — back to the tavern vocabulary, I'm afraid. The realm has no 'rules.' It has statutes, articles, edicts, and customs, each with a different weight and a different remedy. 'Rules' is what children are given before supper so they do not fall down stairs. What you hold, precisely, is an instrument of *police*, executing the enforcement articles of a treaty. And the tell sits in the very line you read. A decree of war names an *enemy* — the Conclave, the northern lords, the said parties. This one names no one. It names an *offense*. Wars are fought between parties. Police is exercised against practices. That distinction has hanged more forgeries than any seal ever has."

He rose — the knees filed their customary complaint — and paced. Three steps. Turn.

"Now the part Bellen will not enjoy, which is the best part. What does the decree *do*? It seizes unlicensed foci and quarters wardens to suppress unregistered magic. And whose register does unregistered magic threaten? The Conclave's. The register is the Conclave's lifeblood — it is what the Conclave purchased at Veyros with its submission to limitation. So the Crown of 863 — or whenever, pending the docket — is spending its own gold and its own officers to protect its rival's monopoly. If the war were cold, hot, or merely cool to the touch, the Crown's cheapest weapon would be sitting in the open: license the hedge-mages, arm the Conclave's competitors, gut the register at no cost to the treasury. Instead the Crown quarters wardens, *at expense*, to strangle the Conclave's competition. Enemies do not enforce one another's monopolies. This is not the absence of war — it is the treaty's bargain running precisely as designed: two rivals jointly suppressing the third thing that threatens them both. You handed me a stone this morning and asked how it disagreed with the mountain. It does not disagree. It *is* the mountain."

He stopped, held up the honesty finger, which trembled slightly on principle.

"He will rally. He will say: *an armed peace, a garrisoned peace, wardens on the boundary stones — is that your peace, Maester?* And the answer is yes, and I will say so in print. Trust is not an instrument of state; machinery is what states use in trust's place. The enforcement articles are not the residue of war — they are its *substitute*. The alternative to quartered wardens is raised levies, and you will find me the one and never the other. A fence is not a feud. He has mistaken the treaty's teeth for the war's breath, and that is a category error dressed up as a discovery."

Then he went to the shelf and — without consulting any catalogue, because he had filed it himself and his memory, unlike his eyes, still kept its appointments — pulled down a slim grey-papered pamphlet and set it on the desk with a thump.

"Filed under T. As I told you. Twice, now. Page three, paragraph two, catalogs the peacetime instruments drafted in war forms — seizures of unlicensed foci, quartering of wardens, restriction of unregistered practice. I described this decree's *genus* ten years before Bellen copied it. He has not read this. None of them have. That is the entire strategy of the modern heresiarch: publish where the rebuttals are not read. You will read it. Tonight. All of it. I will take my wager's winnings in the only coin I accept, which is your attention."

He pulled a clean sheet across the desk.

"I told you this morning to draft Bellen a note yourself. I have revised my estimate of your prose. You will take it down instead — no adjectives; adjectives are where weak cases go to hide. *Line one: your exhibit grounds the Crown's authority in the Treaty of Veyros, which your paper holds never signed. See the enacting clause, in your own copy.* Line two: *its substance executes the treaty's enforcement articles — seizure of unlicensed foci, quartering of wardens — which is the treaty operating, not the war resumed. See articles nine through twelve.* Line three: *produce the original, docketed by regnal year and place of giving, for examination in this archive, under this light. Or withdraw the exhibit.* Sign nothing. Add nothing. If he answers with another copy, you have your answer. A scholar with a document produces it. A scholar with a thesis produces another copy."

He sat, took up his stylus, and looked the apprentice over — spectacles pushed up, voice losing exactly one degree of its edge, which was all the change the instrument could manage.

"And that look you are wearing. This morning I told you pride was dying and making room. That is the room being *used*. It will not last — it never does — so enjoy it. You have gone, in one morning, from asking me for the truth to asking a document what it *does*. That is the whole profession, and most people never make the journey."

The stylus pointed at the shelf.

"You still owe me three answers — who made that copy, when, and where the original sleeps — and I have not forgotten, and I notice you have not remembered. Until they arrive, your conclusion stays what it is: a correct answer that reached you by luck, and luck is not a method. It will be re-derived from the original before either of us spends it. Now. Scroll five. The vellum and I are both still waiting, and only one of us is patient."

Mark the pincer, because it is the shape of every good refutation: either your copy is faithful, and the chancery of 863 called the treaty signed — in which case his own document executes him — or the copy is corrupt, in which case he has brought a rumor to a mountain fight and possesses no exhibit at all. There is no third door. He dies by his own sword or he arrives unarmed. Ten years I have argued this. It is the first time the other side has supplied the blade."

He held up one finger — *but* — and the finger trembled slightly with the effort of honesty.

"I will not hang a hat on wording I have not seen in an original hand, and neither will you, because I am training you to be suspicious even of gifts. Two things live in that clause, and they must be weighed separately. The *form* — an enacting clause invoking the Treaty — is formulaic. Copyists do not invent formulas; they inherit them. If the copy has any fidelity whatsoever, the invocation is original, and the invocation is the part that convicts. Chanceries lie in their prose, never in their forms — I told you that within the hour, and here is why it matters. The *wording*, however — 'signed in 847 AE' — smells. A chancery hand cites 'the Treaty of Veyros' and, if it dates the thing at all, dates it by regnal year, not like a market ledger. That bald '847' has the savor of a modern gloss, some copyist's clarification slipped in where clarifications go. Which is delicious, if you think about it for two seconds: Bellen's own copyist, transcribing a document meant to prove the treaty unsigned, wrote the word *signed* without his hand trembling. The gloss is a confession. His people know it was signed. They know it the way one knows the sky — so thoroughly that it slips out while they are arguing against it."

He began to pace. Three steps. Turn.

"Bellen will rally — he will say the chancery maintained a legal fiction, citing a treaty all parties knew to be unsigned. Arm yourself before he says it to you. A fiction survives only where both parties profit from it, and the Conclave was the treaty's *other* party and the crown's rival. Sixteen years of Conclave clerks corresponding on the treaty's channels, litigating barley duties on the treaty's foundation, and not once — not in the roll you hold, not in the six-letter mill-lease quarrel, not anywhere in this correspondence — protesting that the floor beneath them was not there. Rivals do not acquiesce to that. If the treaty were void, the Conclave's lawyers would have burned the Crown with its own decree in every tariff dispute of a generation. It would have been their first weapon, not a secret kept damp for a scholar to find. That absence of protest, across forty years of clerks arguing about grain, is the least dramatic evidence in the realm, and it is the strongest."

He stopped, and pointed at the paper in the apprentice's hands.

"Three things, in order. First: the rest of the clause, then the body — what does the decree actually *do*? I will wager the third page of my rebuttal that it restricts unlicensed magic, or quarters wardens on the boundary stones, or seizes the goods of hedge-mages off the Conclave's register. Old forms, peacetime business. If it raises levies or names the Conclave an enemy of the Crown, then I fish. Second: the questions you have not answered and I have not forgotten — who made this copy, when, and where does the original sleep? If the answer is the western cellar, you will observe that I am already seated. Third: when you have those answers, you will draft Bellen a note. Three lines, one citation per line. Tell him his own exhibit grounds the Crown's authority in a treaty it calls *signed*, and demand the original's docket — regnal year and place of giving. Then watch him. A scholar with a document produces it. A scholar with a thesis produces another copy."

He resettled his spectacles and looked the apprentice over, taking in the flush, the trailing voice.

"And stop with the face. You look like a man caught stealing. You have been caught *learning*, which at your age feels identical and is the entire point of the profession. You brought the document, you read the clause, and you let it testify against the position you walked in holding — that is the job. The foolishness you are feeling is pride dying, and it is making room. Better scholars than Bellen have been wrong with less grace."

He sat back down and folded his hands.

"Now. The period after '847.' Find it and read to it. I have waited ten years to hear what comes next in that clause, and I intend to hear every word of it."

For a long moment Tomas did not answer at all. He took off his spectacles, folded them, and laid them on the desk with the deliberate care of a man setting down an instrument he had decided not to use on a student today.

"And there it is," he said. "The question. Not *how do we know* — not *what does the evidence weigh* — but *what's the truth*, demanded in one breath, by a boy holding in his hand a document that answers it and asking me to answer it instead. I told you to read to a period. You have asked me to compress ten years of scholarship into a sentence you can carry to supper. Very well. You will have your sentence. Then you will return to the period."

He rose, because verdicts required standing for, and began to tick the matter off on ink-stained fingers.

"First, the question is wounded, and I repair wounded questions before I answer them. *Real or not.* A treaty is not a ghost, apprentice. It does not fade at dawn. Ask what a chancery clerk would ask, and every part has an answer. Was a treaty *negotiated* at Veyros? Yes — Bellen's own draft proves it; no one drafts articles for a war they intend to keep fighting. That was never in dispute. Was it *signed*? Three attested copies — royal, Conclave, temple — each bearing Aldric's seal and seven signatories' marks. Annalists of three kingdoms writing within living memory of the camp. A man whose hand I shook as a boy, who stood outside those walls. And, as of this morning, a decree grounding the Crown's war powers in a treaty that its own copyist called *signed*. Against all that: one unsigned draft from a cellar famous for damp and for the Letters of King Bren. That is not two sides of a dispute. That is a mountain and a wet hole in the ground. Did it *hold*? Forty-four years — not forty; I said forty this morning as a convenience of speech and I regret it — of tariff schedules, boundary stones, and a mill lease that ran six letters. No levies. No spell-fire. Marriages across the old lines. Did *anyone* in those forty-four years call it void? Not once — not even the Conclave, whose lawyers would have made that their first weapon in every barley dispute of a generation. Rivals do not stand silently on a floor they know is missing. And what ended in 891? An institution, not a treaty — and Mira's edict opens by invoking *the peace secured at Veyros*. One does not invoke a peace that never was. I said it this morning. Her scribe said it first."

He stopped pacing and delivered the sentence as promised, flat and final.

"The Treaty of Veyros was signed in 847, held for forty-four years, and outlived the Conclave that signed it. That is as settled as any question about the human past ever becomes, and I will not dress it up as a mystery in order to seem humble. A man who refuses to answer is a man who has not done the work. I have done the work. It is filed under T."

Then the finger came up again, warning.

"Now, *how* you asked it — because that is where you went wrong, and it is the last error I intend to permit today. *The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another.* Three wounds in eleven words. Do not cite the textbook to me, even in my defense — the textbook is a summary of the authority, written by men who read the record so that others needn't. Cite the copies, or cite nothing. Second: *new evidence*. Newness is not a weight. Gossip is newer than the mountain. Documents are weighed by provenance, attestation, and whether the world behaved as though they were true — and on all three counts the draft loses before breakfast. Third: evidence does not *say* anything. Documents are mute. People with theses speak, and then go looking for documents to stand behind. Read cold, the western papers say only this: here is what the Conclave tried and failed to keep at the table. That is all they have ever said. It took a scholar with an invented phrase — *cold state* — to turn an absence of evidence into a presence of thesis."

He sat back down, slowly, and folded his hands — and then, because honesty was a habit that annoyed him as much as anyone, he added the part the apprentice would not expect.

"And attend to this, so you know I am a scholar and not a partisan wearing a chain. What would move me? Not Bellen's insistence — *evidence*. An original counter-instrument with clean provenance: regnal-year docket, attested hands, a seal struck from the matrix and not copied from one. One Conclave letter, out of forty years of them, protesting the treaty's validity. One muster roll between 847 and 891. One burned field. One line in one northern annal. Bring me any of that and I will reconsider in print, at length, and with the same courtesy I have shown the draft. That is the difference between holding a position and being held by one. In ten years, Bellen has brought me none of it. He brings copies of copies, and a word invented so that the absence of all this could be dressed as a discovery."

He replaced the spectacles and picked up his stylus, which was as close as the matter would come to being closed.

"You ask for the truth as though I keep it in a drawer, next to the fishing tackle I did not require. History does not trade in truth; it trades in weight. But do not mistake that for the fashionable comfort that all weights are equal and every thesis receives a prize. The weight here is not close. If you want certainty that no future parchment could ever disturb, the temple is down the corridor and deals in precisely that merchandise. If you want the farthest reach of honest work — you have heard it, and you watched it being built this morning out of barley tariffs, which is how true things are actually built. Slowly. Tediously. In ledgers."

The stylus pointed at the paper in the apprentice's hands.

"Now. I have given you the decade's answer; you still owe me the morning's. The period after '847 AE,' and then the body of the decree — because *what is the truth* is a question for the end of a career, and *what does this document do* is the question for the beginning of one, and you are at the beginning. Read to the period. The chain stays on. And the vellum, I remind you, is still remembering you."

For once, Tomas made a sound that was almost a laugh — a short exhalation through the nose, the kind a man permits himself once a decade and would deny under oath.

"I wagered the third page of my rebuttal on *one* of three provisions," he said. "Unlicensed magic restricted, wardens quartered, hedge-mage goods seized. The document has supplied all three in a single breath. Note the date, apprentice. Scholars are permitted to enjoy their work exactly this much and no further."

Then the finger came up. "But your sentence is wounded in two places, and I repair wounded sentences before I praise the men who speak them. *It isn't about war at all.* No. It is about the war the way a scar is about the wound — it exists because of the war, it is written in the war's forms, and it executes the war's settlement. The war is gone; its furniture remains, and clerks will dust that furniture for four centuries out of sheer spite. *Enforcing rules* — back to the tavern vocabulary, I'm afraid. The realm has no 'rules.' It has statutes, articles, edicts, and customs, each with a different weight and a different remedy. 'Rules' is what children are given before supper so they do not fall down stairs. What you hold, precisely, is an instrument of *police*, executing the enforcement articles of a treaty. And the tell sits in the very line you read. A decree of war names an *enemy* — the Conclave, the northern lords, the said parties. This one names no one. It names an *offense*. Wars are fought between parties. Police is exercised against practices. That distinction has hanged more forgeries than any seal ever has."

He rose — the knees filed their customary complaint — and paced. Three steps. Turn.

Maester Tomas set the rag-paper copy down with a sharp sniff, as though the thing had offended him merely by continuing to exist. He did not look at the apprentice at once; his clouded gaze drifted to the low shelf where the surviving Conclave rolls lay bundled in waxed cloth, their labels faded to ghosts.

“‘Corroborate,’” he repeated, tasting the word and finding it insufficient, “or ‘tell a different story’? There is your imprecision again, apprentice. Archives do not tell stories. They contain records, and records must be authenticated, dated, collated, and weighed. But if you must have a verb, then yes: they corroborate the royal archives. And no, they do not tell a different story, unless by ‘different’ you mean ‘the same peace recorded by the party that lost the war, with more complaining and fewer seals.’”

He turned, squinting, and jerked his chin toward the shelf.

“The Conclave’s own records—what little survived Queen Mira’s dissolution in 891 AE—are not a rival narrative. They are the paperwork of compliance. The twentieth article required the registration of every staff and familiar. The twenty-second dissolved the private retinues of the battle-mages. The reparations schedule assessed silver for Ostwick and the Marcher villages. And what do the Conclave’s surviving rolls contain? Registries. Licences. Ledgers of payment. Joint commissions issued with royal pursuivants to hunt down those who refused to swear. The Conclave did not spend forty-four years pretending it was still at war. It spent forty-four years obeying a treaty it disliked, and hanging the fools who would not.”

He tapped the table with a stained fingernail.

“You ask whether they tell a different story because Bellen has told you they do. But the western fragments are not the Conclave’s central records. They are provincial debris from the western marches—drafts, proposals, private memoranda of envoys urging terms that were later altered or struck out. The Conclave’s own instrument of ratification, sealed with its great seal, was deposited in the temple registries of Veyros. That is where a scholar looks for the architecture of peace, not in a damp chest in the west where a clerk two generations later copied a date he could not read and drew a seal in red chalk.”

He leaned forward, breath whistling through his ink-stained beard.

“If by ‘different story’ you mean that the Conclave resented the settlement, that its members grumbled, that some fled to the hills and burned granges rather than register their staves—then yes, the records tell that story. But that is not a different story about how the war ended. It is the same story: a defeated magical corporation being made to submit to terms it had sworn to accept. Resentment is not belligerency. A grudge is not a campaign. A warrant is not a war.”

He straightened, wincing as his spine protested the motion.

“So here is your answer, precisely. The Conclave’s records corroborate the royal archives on every material point: the Treaty of Veyros was real, it was ratified, and it was enforced. They do not corroborate the western fragments, because the fragments are not Conclave records in the proper sense; they are the litter of negotiation mistaken for the absence of agreement. The war ended in 847 AE. The peace was fragile, sullen, and expensive. It was not a continuation of the war, and Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in 891 AE was administration, not armistice.”

He picked up the topmost Veyrosi letter and held it out, though he did not quite look at the apprentice.

“Now. Take the letter of the third of the Reaping Moon, 848 AE. Extract the clause on the Ostwick assizes. List every defendant, every fine, every surrender, and every reference to the twentieth article. Cross-reference the names with the Conclave’s staff registries, if you can find them unchewed by rats. If you find an army, a muster roll, or a repudiation of Veyros by the Conclave itself, bring it to me and I will revise the canon. If you find only warrants, fines, and grumbling oath-breakers, then you will have your answer. Catalog.”

Maester Tomas did not look up at once. From the far table came the whisper of vellum and the small metallic scrape of a stylus drawn from a satchel, and for a moment he only breathed through his ink-stained beard, shoulders rising and falling as the candle flame guttered. When he spoke, it was to the air above his manuscript, as though correcting a marginal note left by a careless predecessor.

“‘So complete,’” he repeated, and the words were a dry rasp. “I did not say complete. I said they corroborate the royal archives on the material points: ratification, deposit, performance, and enforcement. Those are not the same thing, and the difference is not pedantry—it is the whole of archival method. The Conclave’s surviving rolls are fragmentary, damnably so. Whole decades are missing. The western chapters’ registries were lost to damp, fire, and the enthusiastic neglect of three successive archivists. The temple copies at Veyros were defaced during the Schism of the Seventeenth Year. What remains agrees with the crown’s records. That is corroboration, not completeness. Do not inflate my words to make them easier to knock down.”

He turned then, slowly, the clouded lenses of his spectacles catching the light as he squinted toward the far table where the scroll lay open.

“As for why Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891 AE—because a corporation is not an army, apprentice, and the revocation of a charter is not the cessation of a war. You are conflating two distinct legal acts. The Third Magical War ended when Aldric II and the Conclave made peace at Veyros in 847. The Conclave did not vanish. It persisted as a chartered body: it held property, collected dues from its members, kept its own courts for minor disciplinary matters, licensed blood-rites under the twenty-second article, and—this is the crux—it continued to interpret the treaty’s obligations, often, I am sorry to say, in its own favor. For forty-four years it was a regulated corporation, not a belligerent power. It was disarmed in the sense that its private retinues were dissolved and its staves registered. It was not abolished.”

He tapped the table with a stained fingernail, the rhythm sharp with impatience.

“By the reign of Queen Mira, that arrangement had become an anomaly no sovereign with a spine would tolerate. The crown was enforcing a peace through a body that still behaved, in its own chambers, like a state within a state. The precipitating cause, if you must have a scandal to make it vivid, was the audit of 889 AE. The royal exchequer discovered that the Conclave’s registries had undercounted the staff-tithe by nearly a third for eleven consecutive years, and that certain western chapters had issued licenses to men who had never sworn the peace at all. The Conclave called it clerical error. The crown called it evasion. Mira did not muster an army. She issued a writ of dissolution, seized the Conclave’s assets to satisfy the arrears, and transferred its registries to the royal pursuivants and the new Office of Thaumaturgical Regulation. The Conclave’s own wardens helped pack the ledgers. No campaign chest was opened. No declaration of hostilities was published. The instrument of 891 calls them ‘our late corporation of mages,’ not ‘our late enemies.’ Language, apprentice. It matters.”

He leaned back, wincing as his spine protested the motion.

“So the point was sovereignty and administration, not conquest. Mira abolished a chartered corporation that had already been disarmed, bound, and regulated for two generations. If the war had truly continued in a ‘cold state’ until 891, as Bellen’s fragments would have it, then the dissolution should be accompanied by terms of surrender, a repudiation of Veyros, or a declaration that the Conclave had been an enemy state. We find none of those things. We find a charter being revoked because the corporation had become corrupt, redundant, and expensive. That is not a peace treaty ending a war. That is a queen tidying her realm.”

He waved a hand toward the scroll now lying open on the far table.

“You have your stylus out. Use it. Take the letter of the third of the Reaping Moon, 848 AE. Extract the clause on the Ostwick assizes. "He agrees with me down the page. 'Pendant.' 'Impression sharp.' 'Tag intact.' The cross-reference to item 201 — arithmetic and all. Every particular, to the letter." His eyes opened. "And he corrects me in one."

Then I recited from memory, and my memory seated the copy where the original sits — because I have told this story a hundred times in eleven years, and somewhere in the counting the two changed chairs. Memory is a chronicle, apprentice. It copies itself, and every copying errs. One chronicle counted thrice — I have said it all evening about dead men. Tonight the chronicle was me."

"I promised my thanks, once, to whoever caught a divergence between my recitation and the page. The catalogue has earned it." A pause. "Thank you," he said, to the book.

Enunciation is merely how the trade sounds." A beat. "You read steadily, at least. I noticed. I decline to say so twice."

He rubbed his temple, once, and pressed on.

"Now mark why the correction matters — it explains your sheet of paper down to its last flaw. Autumn court, 863: the chancery certified a copy and entered it in the register. That is the enrollment I described — public, filed, unread by anyone with a chronicle to finish. Your Bellen's sheet descends from item 215, or from some hand that copied 215 — the third remove, at the most generous count. And observe what each remove costs. The original carries wax. The certified copy carries ink *describing* wax. Your sheet carries a painted roundel, because its maker stood at the third remove copying a description of a description. Wax does not survive inking, apprentice. Your document is not a forgery and never was. It is a great-grandchild. It has the family face and none of the family's standing."

Maester Tomas did not answer at once. He drew the green binding back, angled it to the candle, and read the entry himself — twice, slowly, one fingertip beneath each line, as though the page might amend itself under inspection.

"Yes," he said at last. "This is it. Item 210. The pulse, of which I spoke." He looked up. "And now — a remark I cannot number. Nine errors tonight, and then a 'so polite' that is not wrong, merely small. You have commented on the upholstery, apprentice. The house remains unvisited."

He held up one finger before the obvious objection could form.

"Sit with the politeness until it stops surprising you. Correspondence between armed powers is *always* courteous. Courtesy is not softness here; it is distance. Two neighbors disputing a fence write each other insults. Two states disputing a war write each other 'regrets.' The more dangerous the disagreement, the deeper the bow — and I will note, since the granary does not say it, that the Conclave in 890 held no army worth the word. I mark that as inference. But mark this as text: a refusal one can afford to be polite about is still a refusal."

He began to count on his fingers, clause by clause.

"'Regret to inform' — the bow. 'Effective immediately' — the operative clause; hold it; I am returning there. 'Are *not possible*' — and there is the grammar, always the grammar. Not 'we will not extend.' Not 'the Conclave refuses.' *Are not possible*, written the way one writes weather. The commissioners reported their own decision as though it were fog rolling in — because one does not argue with fog, and one cannot hang fog for treason. The passive voice, apprentice, is where refusals go to avoid being hanged."

The stylus tapped once against the binding.

"And then three words you read straight past: '*suspension of arms.*' One cannot suspend what is not raised. The phrase presupposes a state of war standing between Crown and Conclave in the spring of 890 — presupposes it as a bridge presupposes a river. Nobody disguised it because nobody thought it needed disguising. To the men who wrote and filed this letter, it was not a revelation. It was bookkeeping. That is precisely what makes it testimony."

"Now '*effective immediately.*' The fourteenth renewal — item 209, 887, three years, as all of them ran — expired by its own terms. The fifteenth was due. The Conclave declined, and declined at once. So the suspension did not lapse at the end of some grace period; it died the day this letter crossed the Crown's desk. And from that day until the dissolution — the better part of a year — the realm stood in a state of war with *nothing suspended at all*. Threshing went on. Weddings went on. The realm spent the winter of 890 legally at war and noticed nothing, because law and life keep separate ledgers, and only one of them survives in a granary."

He closed the binding, deliberately, and rested his hand upon it.

"Mark the symmetry, because no examination ever will. In 847 the realm stopped fighting and remained at war. In 890 it remained at war and stopped pausing. Neither year looks like a war. Both are."

"Then 891. Mira dissolved the Conclave, and a war whose second party ceases to exist is extinguished — I have given you that distinction already, free of charge, which should make you suspicious of it. Did this letter *cause* her? A year stands between the refusal and the dissolution; the sequence is documentary. The motive is not. No granary in the western marches holds Queen Mira's reasons. Sequence is what parchment can testify to. Motive is what scholars supply — and honest scholars supply it marked as guesswork. Those who do not, build history the way your sheet of paper was built: a copy of a copy of a guess, arriving with a painted seal on it."

He pushed the candle a half-inch from the binding — a correction, not a courtesy — and folded his hands.

"I asked you one letter ago what the *absence* of a fifteenth renewal has to do with everything. You answered that the refusal was polite. That is a remark about the envelope. The question concerns the letter. You have now read item 210 twice, and heard it dissected once. Answer."

“I don’t know.”

Noor looked past the source, toward the dark road, the reservoir, the trees. “Who has your phone?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then why should I believe you?”

The source’s breath fogged. “Because I’m here. Because I told you the manifest line. Because if I wanted you dead, I would have left the trailhead where it was.”

Noor’s throat tightened.

“You put the driver’s name on the drive,” Noor said.

The source looked at the truck.

“No,” they said. “I didn’t.”

“Noor’s voice went flat. “Then who did?”

“Someone used my computer after I left it. I created the folder as a warning. I didn’t know your driver was there. I saw the truck from the ridge. I saw someone in the cab. I didn’t know it was you until the folder appeared.”

Noor’s hand ached around the poker.

“You saw the cabin.”

“I saw the cabin. I saw the truck. I saw the window.”

Noor’s mind snapped back to the half-open window above the kitchen sink.

“Which window?” Noor asked.

“The kitchen.”

Noor did not move.

“The window was open,” they said.

The source went very still.

“Not now,” the source said. “That was before.”

Noor’s breath came out hard.

“You watched the cabin.”

“I had to know you were safe.”

“You didn’t tell me.”

“I was late.”

Noor took one step closer, then stopped.

“Where are the files?” Noor asked.

The source reached into their jacket.

Noor lifted the poker.

The source froze.

“Slow,” Noor said.

The source withdrew a small waterproof pouch. Inside was a thumb drive, black, unmarked, and cold.

“Second copy,” the source said. “Manifest only. Names. Dates. Bank transfers. The minister’s driver. The ghost. The editor.”

Noor looked at the pouch.

“Why did you bring it here?”

“Because if I don’t, I’m not the source. I’m just another person who knows your name.”

Noor’s jaw tightened.

“Give it to me.”

The source set it on the wet concrete between them.

Noor did not pick it up. They looked at the source’s face under the hood. The source was older than Noor remembered, or maybe fear made everyone older. There was a cut along one brow, dried dark, and the source’s left hand kept trembling.

“You’re hurt,” Noor said.

“I’m fine.”

“You’re lying.”

“I’m alive.”

Noor finally bent and picked up the pouch with two fingers. They put it into their pocket without opening it.

“Walk to the truck,” Noor said.

The source did not move.

“No,” the source said. “I’m not getting in.”

Noor’s eyes narrowed.

“Why?”

“Because if your driver is in that truck, I can’t be seen with you.”

Noor looked back at the truck. The cab was dark. The dome light was off. Noor could not see whether anyone was inside.

Noor walked backward to the truck, keeping the poker visible. They opened the passenger door and climbed in.

Noor shut the door and looked at Driver.

“The source is alive,” Noor said. “But they won’t get in. They think you’re part of this.”

Noor pulled the padded case onto their lap and opened it just enough to show the encrypted drive inside.

“Here’s what we’re doing,” Noor said. “We’re not going to the fire hall. We’re not going to the trailhead. We’re going to the train yard behind the water treatment plant. My uncle used to park there. It’s open, it’s cold, and no one will expect two people in a truck at one in the morning.”

Noor started the engine.

The source appeared at the driver’s side window. Noor rolled the window down two inches.

“You said no lights,” Noor said.

“I said if you see one more car, I’m gone.”

Noor looked past the source.

“Then move,” Noor said. “Because I’m not waiting for someone else to arrive.”

The source moved to the passenger side. Noor rolled that window down two inches.

“Talk through the glass,” Noor said. “You do not open the door unless I tell you to.”

The source nodded.

Noor put the truck in gear.

They drove slowly down the spillway road, the source keeping pace beside the cab, one hand on the mirror housing, the other pressed over their mouth as if trying to keep the cold out. Noor watched the mirrors. The road behind remained dark.

When the reservoir opened into the service lane, Noor turned off the dome light and kept the headlights off as long as the snow allowed.

“You have the manifest?” Noor asked through the window.

“Yes.”

“Did you put my name on the drive?”

“No.”

“Did you put the editor’s name on the drive?”

The source hesitated.

“I put the editor’s name on the manifest,” they said. “Because he signed the transfer that moved the minister’s files.”

Noor’s hands tightened on the wheel.

“You said he was involved.”

“I said he was on the list.”

“Those are different words.”

“Not tonight.”

Noor drove.

The train yard appeared after the water treatment plant, a maze of rusted cars, gravel, and floodlights that buzzed at intervals. Noor pulled behind a stack of freight containers and stopped.

“Stay in the truck,” Noor said.

They got out.

The source was already there, breathing hard, eyes moving to the trees, the fence, the lights.

Noor did not take the poker away.

“Show me the manifest,” Noor said.

The source reached into their jacket again.

Noor’s pulse hammered.

The source withdrew a folded paper, not the thumb drive. They unfolded it with shaking hands. The paper was cold, damp at one corner.

Noor took it.

The first line was the minister’s name.

The second line was the minister’s driver.

The third line was the ghost.

The fourth line was Noor’s editor.

The fifth line was Driver.

Noor stared at it until the letters blurred.

The fear came back, not sharp and sudden this time, but slow and enormous, like water rising under a door.

Noor looked at the source.

“You knew.”

“I suspected,” the source said.

“No.” Noor’s voice went low. “You knew.”

The source did not answer.

Noor folded the paper and put it in their pocket.

“We’re not calling the editor,” Noor said. “We’re not going to the fire hall. We’re not going to the paper.”

The source looked up.

“Noor—”

“No.” Noor’s hands were steady again in that awful way. “If the editor’s name is on the manifest, the editor may be the leak. If the fire hall is where we were supposed to go, someone may be waiting there. If the trailhead was bait, the reservoir may be watched.”

Noor looked at the truck.

“I have one backup drive,” Noor said. “I have the original. I have a manifest that says everyone I trusted was already on a list. And I have three hours before the paper’s night desk closes and the story becomes impossible to kill.”

The source said, “Then we publish now.”

Noor looked at them.

“No,” Noor said. “We verify now.”

They turned and walked back to the truck.

Noor climbed in, pulled the padded case onto the seat, and took out the laptop. They connected the source’s thumb drive through a separate port, then ran the manifest against the file names from the encrypted container.

The names matched.

All of them.

Noor copied the manifest to the external backup. Then they opened the encrypted drive again and, for the first time, typed the decryption password.

The laptop whirred.

The container unlocked.

Inside were files: bank transfers, meeting logs, audio clips, a red folder labeled DRIVER, and a final document titled IF NOOR IS READING THIS.

Noor’s breath stopped.

They opened the document.

The first line read:

If you opened this, the drive was bait.

The second line read:

I’m sorry.

The third line read:

Check the cabin’s window.

@@@

Noor’s eyes stayed on the screen for a second too long. When they looked at Driver, the answer came out too calm.

“It says check the cabin window.”

They turned the laptop so the screen faced away. Their thumb hovered over the trackpad, trembling once before it steadied.

“The source wrote it before the meeting. If I opened the drive, I was supposed to know it was bait. I was also supposed to know the fire hall is not safe.” Noor’s voice dropped. “There’s more. The folder with my name was created by WIRE-4. The source says they didn’t make the DRIVER file. They made a placeholder. They listed everyone at the cabin because they were scared of whoever took the field computer.”

Noor looked toward the two inches of open window.

The source stood in the cold with one hand pressed flat against the door, breath fogging the glass.

“Is that true?” Noor asked.

The source’s eyes moved past Noor, toward the passenger side. “True enough.”

“True enough isn’t the truth.”

Noor turned back to the laptop and typed a command to show the document’s properties.

Created 08:55. Modified 09:19. Author: WIRE-4.

The same machine that had made the folder.

Noor’s stomach tightened. Someone had edited after the source’s last call.

They opened the next line in the document.

The window was open because I opened it. I could not get in. I left the second manifest under the storm pane. If it is gone, the cabin is hot and you are not alone in the logging track. Do not go to the fire hall. The ghost has a sheriff’s badge and a key.

Noor read it twice.

“The source opened the window,” Noor said, voice low. “They left something. If it’s gone, someone was in the cabin after we left.”

Noor looked at the source through the glass.

“Why didn’t you say that at the payphone?”

The source pressed one hand to the window. “Because the line could have been recorded. Because I didn’t know if you were alone.”

“You weren’t supposed to be late.”

“I know.”

“You watched me eat crackers and wait three hours.”

“I know.”

Noor’s hands tightened on the laptop until the hinge creaked.

They reached into the padded case, took out the iron poker, and laid it across their knees. Then they checked the truck mirrors. The train yard was empty. The floodlights buzzed, one dimming and coming back. No headlights moved down the access road.

“Verify the manifest,” Noor muttered to themselves.

They plugged the source’s thumb drive into the read-only blocker and compared hashes to the paper manifest’s scanned copy. The file names matched. The dates matched. The minister’s driver matched. The ghost matched. The editor matched. The fifth name—Driver—matched.

Noor stopped.

They looked at Driver, then at the screen, then at the source.

“You put their name on the paper too,” Noor said.

The source’s eyes dropped.

“Because I saw the truck.”

“You saw a truck. You didn’t know who was in it.”

“I didn’t.”

Noor closed their eyes. For a second, the fear became a cold, bright fact. The story had names. One of them belonged to the person who had driven Noor here without asking questions. Noor wanted to be angry. Anger would have been easier.

They opened their eyes.

“We’re going back to the cabin,” Noor said.

The source knocked once against the window.

Noor rolled it down two inches more.

“You don’t get to knock if you’re going to lie,” Noor said.

“Don’t go back,” the source said.

“Then give me a reason not to go back.”

The source looked past Noor, toward the passenger side. The source’s voice went lower.

“The note is real. I left it under the storm pane at 9:06. I didn’t go in. I didn’t touch the drive. But I saw a man on the porch after I left. He had a radio. He opened the window from inside. That means the cabin was already occupied.”

Noor’s breath stopped.

“A man,” Noor said.

“Tall. Dark coat. He knew the latch.”

“Did he see you?”

“Yes.”

Noor looked at the coffee can on the bench. The dead phone sat inside with the tracker. Noor had sunk it in a culvert. The image came back to them: the black rectangle blinking red under the axle. Someone had attached it while Noor was inside the cabin, while Driver was on the couch, while the source was late.

Noor’s hands were steady.

“Get in,” Noor said to the source.

The source shook their head. “No.”

“No is not an option.”

“If your driver is clean, I’ll wait here.”

Noor looked at Driver. The question sat between them: Is Driver clean? Noor did not know. The manifest said yes, someone thought Driver was relevant. The boot print said someone had been at the porch. The tracker said someone had been under the truck. The source’s fear was not proof, but it was not nothing.

Noor turned the laptop off.

They unplugged the original encrypted drive, slid it into the padded case, and zipped it shut. The external backup stayed in Noor’s jacket. The source’s thumb drive went into the metal pouch with the burner phone. Noor put the pouch in the inside pocket, closest to the body, and felt its weight against their ribs.

Before getting out, Noor opened the bag, found the jar of peanut butter and the cracked spoon, and ate a hard spoonful straight. Then they ate a cracker, chewing slowly because their hands needed something to do.
“I suspected,” the source said
For a second, relief moved through them so sharply it hurt.
Third: a stack of press passes, a key card, and a small black notebook.
The last page had no password, but the first page had a phrase the editor had written years ago and never changed.
I have the poker, the truck, and three hours until the story dies.
